passages.happening:
‘Now these are the names of the tribes’ (verse 1). From north to south the land is divided into equal strips, each running from the eastern border to the western sea: Dan, Asher, Naphtali, Manasseh, Ephraim, Reuben and Judah (verses 1-7). Next to Judah lies the portion set apart for the LORD. ‘In the center will be the sanctuary’ (verse 8). The holy portion is for the priests of Zadok's line, with the sanctuary of the LORD in its center, and beside it the Levites' portion; none of it may be sold or exchanged, ‘for it is holy to the LORD’ (verses 9-14).

The remaining strip is common land for the city, worked by people from all the tribes of Israel (verses 15-20). On either side lies the prince's land (verses 21-22). South of the holy portion come Benjamin, Simeon, Issachar, Zebulun and Gad, down to the southern border (verses 23-29).
passages.hearers:
The allotments are unlike any historical map of Israel. Under Joshua the tribes received territories of different sizes, some east of the Jordan. Here each tribe receives an equal strip, all west of the Jordan. The order is new too. The tribes descended from Jacob's sons by the servant women Bilhah and Zilpah sit at the far north and south, while Judah and Benjamin, the tribes that had stayed loyal to the temple in Jerusalem, sit next to the holy portion. Reuben, Jacob's firstborn who lost his place, is restored next to Judah.

Land in Israel was held from God, who said that the land must not be sold permanently because it is his. Equal portions express the equality of God's people under him. The city stands in common land, not in the holy portion, and is shared by all the tribes, not owned by one tribe or one dynasty.
passages.later: The law said, ‘The land must not be sold permanently, because it is Mine’ (Leviticus 25:23). Joshua divided the land ‘as an inheritance to the nine tribes and the half-tribe of Manasseh’ (Joshua 13:7).
passages.asks: Every tribe received an equal share, and none was left out. Ask where you have felt you had no place among God's people. And ask what it means that God gives each one a share.

passages.happening:
The city has gates on all four sides, three on each. ‘Beginning on the north side, which will be 4,500 cubits long, the gates of the city will be named after the tribes of Israel’ (verse 31): Reuben, Judah and Levi on the north; Joseph, Benjamin and Dan on the east; Simeon, Issachar and Zebulun on the south; Gad, Asher and Naphtali on the west (verses 31-34).

‘The perimeter of the city will be 18,000 cubits, and from that day on the name of the city will be: THE LORD IS THERE’ (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
City gates were the place of public life, where elders sat, courts met and trade happened. Naming twelve gates after the twelve tribes means every tribe has its own entrance and its own place in the city's life. Levi, which has no tribal land, receives a gate.

The book that began with God appearing to exiles by a canal in Babylon, far from the temple, ends with a city whose very name is the presence of God. Jerusalem is not named. The city is known by who lives there.
passages.later: The psalm says of the city of God, ‘God is within her; she will not be moved’ (Psalm 46:5). Revelation pictures a holy city whose twelve gates bear ‘the names of the twelve tribes of Israel’ (Revelation 21:12).
passages.hard:
Will Ezekiel's temple actually be built?

Faithful readers answer differently, and this site takes no side. Many dispensational premillennialists expect a literal temple to be built in a future thousand-year reign of Christ on earth, with the land divided as described; they point to the vision's detailed measurements and to promises made to Israel as a nation. Some scholars read chapters 40 to 48 as a program for the restoration after the exile, an ideal the returning community did not carry out. Many Christian interpreters, in Reformed and other traditions, read the vision as symbolic: a picture of God dwelling with a purified people, fulfilled in Christ, in the church as God's temple, and finally in the new creation, which Revelation describes in Ezekiel's own pictures. Some combine these views.

The question involves wider convictions about the millennium and about Israel and the church, which are second-order matters on which Christians disagree. The vision makes no claim about any modern state, temple or border. All agree on its center: God will dwell with his people.
passages.asks: The city's name is not its own; it is the name of the one who lives there. Ask what your life would be called if it were named for what matters most in it. And ask what it would mean for it to be said of you, the LORD is there.
